doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Sarah Vaughan's genius
summary: Joining Vaughan in 1960; she taught him listening to harmonies, sang reed parts at Birdland and took 19 takes for Billy May.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: on a regular basis. And then around 1960, February or March, Sarah Vaughan called. Her bass player, Richard Davis, had recommended me to her and I went out with her. And that was fantastic. That was the greatest experience I ever had musically up to that time. I learned more with Sarah Vaughan than I did in all the five years at Juilliard. But she has amassed so much information in her singing and by playing for her and hearing chords and the way she could, she passed that right on to me, just taught me the kind of art of listening to harmonies. She could sing in one note exactly what harmony I was supposed to play. She was a scary lady. I’ll give you an example of how scary she was. We were at Birdland opposite Count Basie’s band. She got worked up one night and she just sat next to each horn player in the reed section and sang their parts to one of the pieces. Each one. She just moved from one to the other and sang their part. That’s how great she was. I don’t know anybody who could do that. But she just sang, while they’re playing, she was singing right next to them. And I was following and listening, just amazed. That lady was a genius. She was born a genius. We played once a recording session for Billy May and she sang “The Green Hills of Summer” and they went over it 19 times. Each time she sang it she sang it impeccably differently. Now I was in the session. That’s what I mean. That’s how great she was. And each one, I think that’s probably why they never put the record out, because whoever had to listen to it couldn’t decide which take was the best take. She sang it 19 times not because anything was bad but they wanted to see if they could get more. She was amazing, really.
